newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia finance leaders to mull integration.
newsitem.headline: Asia finance leaders to mull integration.

text.p: Asian financial leaders meeting in Hong Kong this week are expected to contribute some new ideas on ways to achieve financial integration in the region but few concrete steps.
"I think it will be very difficult for this meeting to come up with any sort of plan," said George Leung, economic adviser to Hongkong Bank.
"But it is important for the countries that participate in the meeting that there is some consensus that they want to cooperate," he said.
The conference on Friday on Asian financial integration is jointly organized by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the International Monetary Fund.
Finance ministers or central bankers from Hong Kong, China, Malaysia, Indonesia, South Korea, the Philippines, Japan, Singapore, Australia and Britain are scheduled to attend.
The one-day get-together comes on the heels of the "Six Markets Meeting" held in Tokyo on Tuesday that grouped Australia, China, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore and the U.S.
Delegates ended the Tokyo meeting with a vow to coooperate to seek stability in currency and other markets in the region but without any agreement on means to that end.
Analysts said they expect the Hong Kong forum to be similarly long on talk and short on action.
"Financial integration is a broad theme that people have been talking about, but it is a slow process," said Paul Alapat, financial economist at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong.
Issues surrounding regional integration and cooperation have loomed large whenever Asian leaders meet and with good reason.
With Europe well on its way to full financial union and the Americas tied through various trade pacts, Asian nations must work together to compete, said Hongkong Bank's Leung.

Regional integration of products markets has been progressing for many years as Asian countries specialise in the portion of the manufacturing process in which they have a comparative advantage, either because of technological know-how, natural resource endowment or labour supply.
Many countries also have made unilateral strides toward integrating with the global financial markets by liberalising domestic markets to allow greater foreign participation.
In financial cooperation, Asian central bankers have signed repurchase agreement pacts to help each other combat foreign exchange volatility in times of crisis.
But financial integration, which could include the standardisation of market procedures across borders and the creation of regional watchdogs, has been a stickier subject.

For example, proposals to create an Asian central bank along the lines of the Bank for International Settlements have met with only lukewarm support, as have suggestions for an Asia-wide securities clearing system.
But analysts said the momentum clearly is toward greater financial integration, even if it doesn't occur right away.
"I'm not sure if the central banks are anywhere near the level where they could work out the details on an Asian BIS, for example," said Lehman's Alapat.
"But what the central banks are saying is, this is our future agenda, this is the direction we want to take," he said.
Friday's meeting also will include discussion of Hong Kong's role in the region in the years to come, a timely subject as the territory prepares to revert to China in July.
"The meeting is a very appropriate channel to send out the message that Hong Kong will remain the same," said Leung.
